name: Cholesterol
lead: Cholesterol is the main sterol in animals: a structural component of cell membranes and a precursor to steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. Nearly all animal cells can make it, with the liver and intestines producing about 80 percent of the daily total.[1]

For appearance, cholesterol matters in two places. In the skin it is one of three principal lipids of the stratum corneum, alongside ceramides and free fatty acids, and this lipid matrix keeps water in and the surface smooth and supple.[1][21] Barrier-repair moisturisers therefore often combine cholesterol with ceramides and fatty acids, and people with dry or irritated skin use them to get a calmer, more even-looking surface.[26] In the body it is the starting material for testosterone and other steroid hormones, which is why it features in physique and diet discussions on looksmaxxing forums.[25][7]

Blood cholesterol is the third context. Elevated LDL cholesterol is a recognised cardiovascular risk factor, and visible cholesterol deposits on the eyelids or tendons (xanthelasma and xanthomas) are one of the few ways high blood lipids show up on the face and hands.[1][24] Researchers have studied blood lipids, diet and exercise extensively, while topical cholesterol used on its own for cosmetic purposes has not been the subject of published trials.[2][10][11]

chain: Cholesterol packs with ceramides and fatty acids in the outer skin layer
The lipid matrix limits water loss
Skin looks and feels smoother and less dry
angle.text: Barrier-repair moisturisers sometimes include cholesterol alongside ceramides and fatty acids to mimic the skin's own lipid mix. People use them on dry, rough or compromised skin to restore a smoother, more hydrated surface. The same molecule is also the starting material for testosterone and other steroid hormones, which is why it comes up in diet and physique discussions.

infobox: Membrane component; precursor of steroid hormones, bile acids, vitamin D[1]
About 25 percent by weight of the stratum corneum lipid matrix, with ceramides and free fatty acids[1]

paras: Synthesis takes roughly 37 steps from acetyl-CoA, with the first 18 following the mevalonate pathway through HMG-CoA reductase, the target of statins. The SREBP pathway, together with SCAP and INSIG-1, senses cellular cholesterol and adjusts production.[1] Cholesterol modulates membrane fluidity and packing and helps form the cholesterol-rich lipid rafts described in a widely cited 1997 Nature review; it also supports myelin insulation of nerves.[1][3]

Cholesterol travels in the blood in lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL). Each LDL particle carries about 1,500 cholesterol ester molecules, and HDL is thought to return cholesterol to the liver in reverse cholesterol transport. The liver converts cholesterol to bile acids, about 95 percent of which are reabsorbed.[1] A 1972 method for estimating LDL concentration without an ultracentrifuge, still one of the most cited papers in the field, made routine lipid panels practical.[4] Grokipedia gives a typical body synthesis of about 700 to 900 mg per day, with dietary intake contributing a smaller share because of feedback inhibition of production.[5]

Animal foods such as red meat, egg yolks, liver, shellfish and butter contain cholesterol; plants contain only small amounts, and plant sterols compete with cholesterol for absorption in the intestine. A typical US man consumes about 307 mg per day, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Testosterone is made from cholesterol: the enzyme CYP11A1 cleaves the cholesterol side chain to form pregnenolone, and further steps lead to androstenedione and testosterone. In men the Leydig cells of the testes produce over 95 percent of it.[25] Regulation is by the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: low testosterone prompts GnRH release, which drives LH and FSH, and rising testosterone feeds back to dampen the signal.[25]

This is the basis of a recurring looksmaxxing debate. Some users argue that eating more cholesterol and fat supports testosterone, while others reply that testosterone is governed by brain signalling and that the body makes ample cholesterol on its own, citing vegans' comparable testosterone levels.[6][7] Wikipedia's testosterone article states that evidence that low-fat diets reduce testosterone is limited,[25] while a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention studies by Whittaker and Wu concluded that low-fat diets appear to decrease testosterone in men, with more randomised trials needed; a correction to that paper was published in 2026.[27] No trial has tested dietary cholesterol on its own against testosterone.

The outer skin layer, the stratum corneum, consists of flattened corneocytes embedded in a lipid matrix of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids. That matrix acts like mortar between bricks, preventing water loss, keeping the layer pliable and excluding irritants and allergens.[21] Wikipedia gives cholesterol as roughly 25 percent of the lipid matrix by weight, with about 50 percent ceramides and 15 percent free fatty acids.[1]

When the matrix is depleted, as in dry or eczema-prone skin, the surface becomes rough and flaky. Reviews of skin-barrier science describe altered lipid composition as a feature of atopic dermatitis and note that ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids are all required for barrier homeostasis.[26] A 1996 paper by Man and colleagues examined how physiological lipid mixtures could be optimised for barrier repair, and later reviews discuss lipid-based barrier-repair therapy.[26]

Commercial barrier-repair emulsions combine ceramides, cholesterol and fatty acids. One reported example is a ceramide-dominant triple-lipid emulsion at a 3:1:1 ratio, which has been evaluated in clinical practice and in a trial against fluticasone in children with atopic dermatitis.[26] Cosmetic-grade moisturisers often list the same three lipids together, and people with dry or compromised skin use them to restore a smoother, more hydrated surface. Published trials focus on atopic dermatitis rather than on cosmetic appearance.[26]

Xanthelasma is a sharply demarcated yellowish collection of cholesterol under the skin, usually on or around the eyelids. Xanthomas are yellowish cholesterol-rich deposits that can appear elsewhere; eruptive xanthomas are linked with high triglycerides, tendon xanthomas of the hands, feet and heels with familial hypercholesterolaemia, and palmar and tuberoeruptive types with type III hyperlipidaemia.[24] People who notice such deposits are commonly assessed for blood lipid disorders, according to the reference summary.[24]

Elevated LDL cholesterol is associated with atherosclerosis, heart attack and stroke, while HDL is thought to carry cholesterol back to the liver. Treatments include diet changes, statins, fibrates, PCSK9 inhibitors and bile acid sequestrants; about 1 in 250 people have familial hypercholesterolaemia. Wikipedia reports that lowering LDL by about 38.7 mg/dL is associated with roughly a 21 percent reduction in cardiovascular events, and that adults are advised to be tested every 4 to 6 years.[1] The NCEP ATP III guideline is a landmark framework for detecting and treating high blood cholesterol in adults.[2][8]

A 2025 individual-patient-data meta-analysis in JAMA Cardiology compared alternative LDL-lowering strategies with high-intensity statins in people with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.[28] The Framingham risk profile is a widely used tool for converting cholesterol and other markers into a cardiovascular risk estimate, and Wikipedia reports an association between each 10 mg/dL rise in total cholesterol and a 9 percent rise in 30-year cardiovascular mortality in that cohort.[1][9]

Many appearance-minded people meet cholesterol as a blood-test number that interacts with diet, training and any hormone use. Wikipedia also notes that low cholesterol is associated with some conditions, often as a consequence of illness, and that Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome is a genetic disorder of cholesterol synthesis.[1]

A systematic review of 37 guidelines, 108 systematic reviews and 20 randomised trials found that foods high in unsaturated fat and low in saturated and trans fat, foods with added plant sterols or stanols, and foods high in soluble fibre such as oats, barley and psyllium lowered LDL cholesterol by at least moderate amounts (0.20 to 0.40 mmol/L). Unfiltered coffee raised it.[10]

A 2025 meta-analysis of 148 randomised exercise trials covering 8,673 participants found modest improvements of roughly 3.5 to 11.7 percent in total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides and VLDL with aerobic, resistance or combined training.[11] A meta-analysis of 28 trials with 1,924 participants examined psyllium fibre and LDL cholesterol, non-HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B.[12]

Dietary cholesterol itself has a contested record. A 2022 analysis of 27,078 men in the ATBC cohort, with a meta-analysis of cohort studies, reported that each additional 300 mg per day of dietary cholesterol was associated with hazard ratios of 1.10 for overall and 1.13 for cardiovascular mortality.[13] A 2025 randomised crossover study of 61 adults compared dietary cholesterol from eggs with saturated fat for effects on LDL, motivated by evidence that saturated fat has the larger effect.[14]

Guidance has shifted over time. The 1977 US Senate Dietary Goals recommended reducing cholesterol consumption to 300 mg daily,[23] and Wikipedia reports that the 2015 US guidelines dropped the numerical 300 mg limit while advising people to eat as little dietary cholesterol as possible.[1] A 2013 AHA/ACC report prioritised healthy dietary patterns such as DASH and Mediterranean diets.[1]

sections.h: Diet culture and the carnivore diet
paras: Cholesterol turns up in meat-heavy and low-carbohydrate diet communities, where followers often describe high cholesterol as harmless or even beneficial, while cardiology guidance continues to treat elevated LDL as a risk factor.[16][22] The carnivore diet has historical roots in the 19th century, with Arnaldo Cantani's animal-based regimen for diabetic patients in the 1870s and James Salisbury's lean-beef diet in the 1880s, and was popularised online from 2018 by Shawn Baker, with Jordan and Mikhaila Peterson as prominent adherents and Paul Saladino promoting an animal-based variant in 2024.[22] Wikipedia states that the diet raises LDL cholesterol, and dietetic organisations such as the British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia have criticised it.[22]

A 2025 case reported in JAMA Cardiology and covered by the press described a man who ate several pounds of butter, cheese and burgers a day for eight months and developed yellowish cholesterol deposits on parts of his body; the story circulated widely on Lemmy and Hacker News.[15][16][29] Hacker News discussions of cholesterol, inflammation and saturated fat, from a 2012 thread on how fat and cholesterol came to be viewed as harmful to a 2025 thread on inflammation as a heart-disease predictor, show how contested lay interpretations remain.[17][30]

Francois Poulletier de la Salle identified cholesterol in gallstones in 1769, and Michel Eugene Chevreul named it cholesterine in 1815; the name derives from Greek words for bile and solid. Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen shared the 1964 Nobel Prize for work on cholesterol and fatty-acid metabolism, and Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein won in 1985 for the SREBP regulatory pathway.[1]

Grokipedia also credits Nikolai Anitschkow's 1913 rabbit-feeding experiments with establishing a link between cholesterol and arterial disease, and Ancel Keys' Seven Countries Study (1958 to 1970) with shaping early dietary guidelines, while noting methodological critiques of Keys' country selection.[5]

No studies found on topical cholesterol alone for skin appearance. Related human research includes trials of ceramide-dominant triple-lipid barrier-repair emulsions in atopic dermatitis,[26] meta-analyses of diet and exercise effects on blood lipids,[10][11][12] and the Framingham and ATBC cohorts.[9][13] Registered trials address Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, a cholesterol-synthesis disorder, including a 130-participant natural-history study and a 100-participant trial of cholesterol and antioxidant treatment,[18][19] and a withdrawn trial of dietary cholesterol and adipose tissue inflammation.[20]

lore.intro: Cholesterol is discussed on looksmaxxing forums mostly in relation to testosterone, diet and heart risk, usually in combative threads, and in skincare circles as a barrier lipid.[6][7]

claims.claim: Eating more cholesterol and fat raises testosterone
claims.believers: Some gym and diet-oriented posters say high-fat, high-cholesterol eating supports testosterone because the hormone is built from cholesterol.[7]
claims.experts: Other forum users counter that testosterone is governed by pituitary and hypothalamic signalling and that the body synthesises ample cholesterol, pointing to studies of vegans' testosterone.[7][25] A 2021 meta-analysis reported lower testosterone on low-fat diets, but no trial has tested dietary cholesterol directly against testosterone.[27]

claims.believers: Forum posters joke about doctors who call cholesterol 'bad', and carnivore-diet communities describe elevated cholesterol as benign.[6][16]
claims.experts: Guidelines such as ATP III treat high LDL as a cardiovascular risk factor,[2] and a cohort analysis associated higher dietary cholesterol and egg intake with higher overall and cardiovascular mortality.[13]

claims.claim: Cholesterol-rich skincare repairs the skin barrier
claims.believers: Brands and users of barrier-repair creams say adding cholesterol with ceramides and fatty acids mimics the natural lipid mix and restores smoothness.[26]
claims.experts: The role of cholesterol in the barrier is well described,[1][21] and ceramide-dominant triple-lipid emulsions have been trialled in atopic dermatitis,[26] but no cosmetic trial of topical cholesterol alone has been published.

claims.claim: Dietary cholesterol from eggs is not what drives blood LDL
claims.believers: Egg-eating lifters and low-carb communities argue that dietary cholesterol has little effect on blood cholesterol, and long-running online threads question how saturated fat and cholesterol came to be seen as harmful.[30]
claims.experts: A 2025 crossover trial in 61 adults separated egg cholesterol from saturated fat motivated by evidence that saturated fat has the larger LDL effect, while a cohort meta-analysis linked dietary cholesterol to mortality.[13][14]

claims.claim: Carnivore-diet cholesterol deposits show the diet is harmful or harmless
claims.believers: Carnivore advocates describe high LDL as a benign or even protective adaptation, while critics online point to the 2025 case of deposits on the skin.[16][29]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the diet raises LDL cholesterol and that dietetic bodies criticise it; xanthomas are described in reference sources as associated with hyperlipidaemia.[22][24]

claims.claim: Inflammation matters more than cholesterol for heart disease
claims.believers: A widely shared 2025 Hacker News thread debated claims that inflammation predicts heart disease more strongly than cholesterol.[17]
claims.experts: Guidelines continue to treat LDL as a primary treatment target, and statin and non-statin LDL-lowering trials report cardiovascular outcomes.[2][28]

card.summary: The body's key membrane sterol and a third of the skin's barrier lipid mix; in skincare it shows up alongside ceramides, with no appearance trials on its own.
card.note: Blood cholesterol and topical cholesterol are different topics; heart-health guidance concerns the former.

quick.overview:
Cholesterol is a waxy lipid every animal cell uses. In skin it forms part of the lipid mortar, with ceramides and fatty acids, that holds water in.
Barrier-repair creams sometimes include it for that reason, but there are no appearance trials of topical cholesterol.
quick.mechanism: In the stratum corneum it packs with ceramides and fatty acids into ordered layers that limit water loss. In the body it is a precursor to hormones, bile acids and vitamin D.
quick.risks: High blood LDL cholesterol is linked to heart disease and is treated under clinical guidelines. Topical cosmetic use has not been assessed.
